newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia govt plans savings incentives - paper.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia govt plans savings incentives - paper.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello is planning to launch a family savings incentives package in next year's budget, The Australian newspaper reported on Monday.
Costello would pay for the incentive plan by using A$4.3 billion of funds that had been set aside by the former Keating Labor government to pay for a second round of tax cuts, the newspaper said.
Costello was currently considering a major report on options for promoting savings that was prepared by a special inter-departmental committee, The Australian said.

"The report to the Treasurer assumes that all the A$4.3 billion tax cuts due in July 1998 will be committed to any new savings initiatives, as they were fully factored into the four year budget plan delivered in August," the newspaper said.
"The Treasurer is understood to favour a special savings scheme for parents concerned about the high cost of their children's education," it said.
The Keating-planned tax cuts, the second of two rounds, were to be paid into workers superannuation accounts between 1998 and 2000.

Costello was careful in the August budget not to say whether his government would abandon the second round of tax cuts or what might be done with the extra forecast revenue if they were not implemented.

The Australian also said that the government had directed that the Treasury's preperation of the mid-year economic and fiscal update be accelerated so it can be completed before Christmas instead of wating until January.

"The Treasurer is keen to deliver another round of substantial budget cuts to boost the government's credibility in the business community and financial markets, with a minimum two year target of A$1 billion to A$2 billion considered appropriate in senior government ranks."
Costello said in August that the goverment would decide in 1997 on any further measures beyond the A$7.2 billion of deficit cuts over two years announced in the August 1996 budget.
The government had promised A$8 billion of cuts over two years soon after its March election.
Currently the government is forecasting a A$5.6 billion underlying deficit in the year to June 30, 1997, a A$1.5 billion deficit in 1997/98 and a A$1 billion surplus in 1998/99.
